title: Sequence modelling and the limits of recurrent networks

slides.title: What is sequence modelling?
bullets: Sequences have variable length and order matters
Examples: text, speech, time series
Feed‑forward nets cannot handle variable length
slides.notes: Introduce the idea that many tasks involve sequences: text, speech, time series. Explain that a sequence model must capture order and variable length. Mention that students have seen feed‑forward nets but those cannot handle variable‑length input. This sets up why recurrent architectures were developed.

slides.title: Recurrent neural network (RNN) basics
bullets: Hidden state updated each time step
Same weights reused across steps
Output can be produced at every step
slides.notes: Describe the RNN recurrence: h_t = f(W_hh h_{t-1} + W_xh x_t). Emphasize weight sharing across time steps, which gives parameter efficiency but creates a deep computational graph when unrolled. Note that the hidden state is the only memory passed forward.

slides.title: Encoder‑decoder translation with RNN
bullets: Encoder reads source tokens sequentially
Final hidden state becomes context vector
Decoder generates target conditioned on context
slides.notes: Walk through the classic encoder‑decoder architecture for machine translation. The encoder reads the source sentence token by token, updating its hidden state. After the last source token, the final hidden state becomes the context vector c. The decoder is another RNN initialized with c and generates the target sentence one token at a time.

slides.title: Worked example: translating "I love you"
bullets: Encoder produces hidden states h1, h2, h3
Context vector c equals final hidden state h3
Decoder starts from c and emits "Je"
Decoder continues with "t'aime"
slides.notes: Use a concrete short sentence pair to illustrate the flow. Show how the encoder produces hidden states h1, h2, h3 for 'I love you'. The context vector c = h3 is passed to the decoder, which then emits 'Je', 't', 'aime'. Point out that all source information must be compressed into c, which becomes a bottleneck for longer sentences.

slides.title: Fixed‑size context vector is a bottleneck
bullets: Context vector dimension does not grow with source length
Long sentences force compression into same vector
Information loss limits translation quality
slides.notes: Explain that the context vector has fixed dimensionality regardless of source length. As the source grows, the encoder must squeeze more information into the same vector, causing loss of detail. This is the information bottleneck that motivated attention.

slides.title: Vanishing gradient problem in deep unrolled RNNs
bullets: Gradients multiplied by same matrix many times
Vanishing gradients erase long‑range signals
Exploding gradients cause unstable training
slides.notes: When the RNN is unrolled for many steps, gradients are multiplied by the same weight matrix repeatedly. If the spectral radius is <1, gradients vanish; if >1, they explode. Both make learning long‑range dependencies hard. The sequential nature also prevents parallel computation on GPUs.

slides.title: LSTM and GRU mitigate but do not eliminate the issues
bullets: Gating creates near‑constant gradient paths
Still process tokens sequentially
Final hidden state remains a single vector
slides.notes: LSTM and GRU introduce gating mechanisms that create paths with near‑constant gradient flow, alleviating vanishing gradients. However, they still process tokens sequentially and still compress the entire source into a final hidden state, so the bottleneck remains for very long sequences.

slides.title: Training difficulty for very long sequences
bullets: Memory for back‑propagation grows linearly
Gradient paths stay long despite gating
Difficulty varies with task and model size
slides.notes: Even with gated units, training on very long sequences is difficult: memory for back‑propagation through time grows linearly, gradient paths remain long, and optimization can stall. The severity depends on the specific task, model size, and training tricks such as gradient clipping.

slides.title: Check: Identify the encoder‑decoder bottleneck

quiz.question: What is the main limitation of the fixed‑size context vector in an RNN encoder‑decoder?
options: It forces the decoder to generate tokens in parallel
It compresses the entire source sequence into a single vector
It eliminates the need for backpropagation through time
quiz.explanation: The context vector is a bottleneck because all source information must be compressed into one fixed‑size vector, limiting long sequences. The tempting wrong option about parallel generation is incorrect because RNN decoders generate sequentially, not in parallel.

slides.notes: This question checks whether students understand that the fixed‑size context vector is the bottleneck. The correct answer highlights compression; the distractor about parallel generation is a common misconception because attention later enables parallelism.

slides.title: Why attention helps: soft lookup instead of hard bottleneck
bullets: Decoder query attends to all encoder states
Attention weights produce a dynamic context
No single vector must hold everything
slides.notes: Introduce attention as a soft lookup: at each decoder step, a query vector is compared to all encoder hidden states (keys) to produce attention weights. The weighted sum of values yields a context vector that changes per decoding step, removing the single‑vector bottleneck.

slides.title: Information flow comparison: RNN vs Attention
bullets: RNN path length grows with sequence length
Attention gives constant‑length paths
Attention enables parallel computation
slides.notes: Compare the two architectures on three dimensions. RNN encoder‑decoder has a path length proportional to sequence length, strictly sequential decoding, and a single fixed context. Attention provides constant‑length paths, enables parallel computation across heads, and yields a dynamic context per target token.

slides.title: Check: Attention advantage over RNN bottleneck

quiz.question: How does attention address the bottleneck of the encoder‑decoder RNN?
options: By using a larger fixed‑size vector
By allowing the decoder to attend to all encoder hidden states at each step
By training the decoder without gradients
quiz.explanation: Attention computes a weighted sum of all encoder hidden states, giving the decoder direct access to the whole source sequence. Option A is wrong because attention does not rely on a single fixed‑size vector.

slides.notes: This question verifies that students grasp the key advantage of attention: direct access to all encoder states. The distractor about a larger fixed vector is plausible but incorrect because attention does not rely on a single vector.

slides.title: Key takeaways
bullets: RNNs process sequences step by step with a hidden state
Encoder‑decoder compresses source into one context vector
Fixed‑size vector creates an information bottleneck
Vanishing/exploding gradients hinder long‑range learning
LSTM/GRU improve gradients but not the bottleneck
Attention removes the bottleneck with dynamic soft lookup
slides.notes: Recap the main points: RNNs process sequences step by step with a hidden state; encoder‑decoder compresses the source into one vector; this creates an information bottleneck and vanishing‑gradient problems; LSTM/GRU help gradients but not the bottleneck; attention solves both by letting the decoder attend to all encoder states dynamically.
